Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 64 (al-Taghabun), verse 1:

﴿He is glorified by whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth. To Him belongs dominion, and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things capable.﴾

Since most of what this surah contains is the refutation of the polytheists' association of partners with God, and their rebuke for the whole of the religion of association along with its offshoots, the greatest of which is their denial of resurrection, their denial of the Messenger ﷺ, and their denial of the Qur'an, and since these are the roots of their error, the surah opens by announcing their misguidance and their ingratitude toward the One who bestowed favours upon them. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies God, exalted above deficiencies, either by the tongue of speech, as the angels and the believers do, or by the tongue of state (lisan al-hal), as the obedience of the obedient among the created beings does, namely the angels and the believers, who perceive. It is also glorified by the tongue of state in the sense that the condition of need for origination and provision points to God, as the need of animals for sustenance and the need of a tree for rain, and what the condition of all those beings testifies to: that they are owned by God and subjected to what He wills for them. None of these created beings has contradicted the indication of its condition by the contradictions of the unbelief of its speech. Therefore no one has departed from this glorification except the people of misguidance among mankind and the devils, for they have been veiled from the testimony of their own condition, since they have covered it with the edifice of unbelief.

So the meaning is: whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies God, while you are contrary to that.

This indicates, first, the establishment of the declaration of God's transcendence and the strength of His dominion, so that those who believe may increase in faith, and it serves as instruction and a favour to them. Second, it indicates by way of allusion (kinaya) an implicit reproach of the polytheists, who did not declare Him transcendent or revere Him, and so they ascribed partners to Him.

The verb of glorification (yusabbihu) is used in the present tense to indicate the renewal and continuance of that glorification, and a parallel to this has already been mentioned at the opening of Surah al-Jumu'ah.

It is used in the opening of the surahs al-Hadid, al-Hashr and al-Saff in the past form (sabbaha), to indicate that the glorification has become firmly established in ancient times. Thus from this variety in the openings of these surahs both meanings are obtained, in addition to what we have explained of the particular connection with Surah al-Jumu'ah, and what is in this surah of the connection between the renewal of glorification and the command to pardon relatives, the command to be mindful of God to the extent of one's capacity, and to hear and obey, so that believers do not suffice themselves with having attained faith, but strive to strengthen it through righteous deeds.

The repetition of (ma), the relative pronoun, in His saying (﴿wa-ma fi al-ard﴾, "and whatever is in the earth") is for the purpose of verbal emphasis (ta'kid lafzi).

The clause (﴿lahu al-mulk﴾, "to Him belongs dominion") is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) occupying the position of a causal justification (ta'lil) and a causal ground (tasabbub) for the content of the glorification by whatever is in the heavens and the earth. For the fact that all existing things are bound up with the indications of God's transcendence, above partners and deficiencies, has no requirement except that He alone possesses and originates them, and that they are in need of Him, and that He disposes of them as an owner who is singular in his dominion.

In this clause there is an honouring of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth for their turning towards the glorification of God and the renewal of that glorification.

The fronting of the predicate over the subject (taqdim al-musnad 'ala al-musnad ilayhi) serves to restrict it to the subject, that is, it restricts the connection of the lam of entitlement to the dominion to Him, exalted is He, so that there is no dominion for anyone else. This is a restriction by claim (qasr idda'i), based on disregarding whatever dominion belongs to others, because of its deficiency and because it is not free of need for another, from whom it is held. This is unlike His dominion, exalted is He, for He is the Absolute King, into whose authority every possessor of dominion enters.

The clause (﴿wa-lahu al-hamd﴾, "and to Him belongs praise") has a content which is the cause of the glorification of God by whatever is in the heavens and the earth, since glorification is part of praise. Therefore it is inevitable that the praise of beings endowed with perception is restricted to Him, since He is the one described by beauty that is chosen and absolute. Thus He is the one truly deserving of praise and glorification.

This restriction is a restriction by claim, on the basis of disregarding the praise of others because of the deficiency of their perfections. If by praise is meant what includes gratitude (shukr), or what leads to it, as in the hadith: "Praise is the head of gratitude; a servant who does not praise God has not thanked Him," and this is what the context requires, by way of making foolish the intellects of the polytheists in their worship of other than Him, then gratitude is also restricted to Him, exalted is He, because He is the true Benefactor with blessings for which no one else has the capacity to bestow, and He is the one who bestows upon benefactors what they bestow outwardly. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from God﴾ [al-Nahl: 53], as has been mentioned in the commentary on the beginning of Surah al-Fatihah.

The clause (﴿wa-Huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir﴾, "and He is over all things capable") is coordinated with the two clauses before it, and it is in the position of a concluding appendix (tadhyil) to them, and an explanation of the basis of the two restrictions in them. For the sense is: over all things He is the possessor of true dominion, and He is the one specially deserving of true praise.

In this concluding appendix there is a promise to the grateful and a threat and warning to the polytheists.

The restriction to the attribute (qadir, "capable") here is because the created beings which glorify God are first indicators of the attribute of power, since whoever observes created beings knows that their Creator is capable.

This is a restatement of what His words ﴿He glorifies Allah, whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ (al-Taghabun 64:1) convey, and a transition to the purpose of that passage, stated explicitly: that those who associate partners with Allah have disbelieved in His blessing and in their own creation, in addition to denying the evidence of His transcendence above the deficiency they ascribed to Him. For this reason He placed ﴿so among you is a disbeliever﴾ before ﴿and among you is a believer﴾, because the first division is the one intended by this statement, both allusively and explicitly.

The definiteness of the two parts in the sentence ﴿He it is who created you﴾ conveys the restriction (qasr, restriction or exclusivity) of the attribute of creating to Allah, the Exalted. It is a real (haqiqi) restriction, intended to allude, by way of kinaya (metonymy, indirect expression), to a rebuttal of the polytheists, who devoted themselves to worshipping idols which they knew had not created them. Such things do not deserve to be worshipped, since worship is gratitude. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who creates not? Will you not then remember?﴾ (al-Nahl 16:17).

The address in His words ﴿created you﴾ is to all people whom the Qur'an calls, as indicated by His words ﴿so among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾, for people do not count these two categories as anything else.

The fa' (so) in ﴿so among you is a disbeliever﴾ is conjunctive, coordinating with the clause ﴿He it is who created you﴾, and it is not coordinating with the verb ﴿created you﴾. It indicates tafri' (consequence) in occurrence without causation.

A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And We placed in their offspring prophethood and the Book, so among them is one who is guided, and many of them are defiant transgressors﴾ (al-Hadid 57:26). Such a consequential construction carries a sense of wonder at the course of some people's conditions contrary to what natural disposition requires: ﴿and you make your provision that you deny?﴾ (al-Waqi'ah 56:82). Thus the clause ﴿so among you is a disbeliever﴾ is the object intended by the consequential structure, and it is consequence in actuality. The mention of the disbeliever is placed first because he is the more important in this context, as His saying indicates: ﴿Has there not come to you the report of those who disbelieved before?﴾ (al-Taghabun 64:5).

The clause ﴿and among you is a believer﴾ is a completion (tatmim) and an honouring of the status of the people of faith, and a contrast between their condition and the condition of the people of disbelief, and a juxtaposition of one condition with the other.

His saying ﴿and Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ is a completion (tatmim), a precautionary qualification (ihtiras), and a digression (istitrad). It completes what perfects the purpose of dividing them into two groups, to show the difference between the two groups in good and evil, and He knows that, and knows that it occurs, and Allah is not overpowered in its occurrence, but His wisdom and knowledge required it. Setting aside detail, this is a lengthy matter which we shall devote to a separate work on the meaning of qadar (divine decree) and the course of people's deeds in this world, if Allah wills. Here we shall limit ourselves to saying: Allah created people

[Page 263]

and deposited in them intellects which, through sound reasoning, reach the knowledge of Allah in the manner befitting Him, free from shortcoming, the impurities of desire, and the veils of obstinacy. He created in them the capacity for righteous deeds and other deeds, which al-Ash'ari called kasb (acquisition) and the Mu'tazilah called the power of the servant (the disagreement concerning the terminology is noted). He guided them to righteousness and warned them against corruption. Allah knows what each person acquires, and had He willed, He would have turned the perpetrator of corruption away from his act. But He brought into being systems, some linked to others and spread out, and His wisdom required the preservation of those many systems, so that nothing obstructs their course along their paths, or nullifies their operation for the sake of reforming individuals who are part of a whole, because general systems are more comprehensive, so preserving their regularity is more beneficial and more weighty. Thus the will and power of Allah do not descend to intervene in what is called kasb according to our principles, or in the created capacity according to the principles of the Mu'tazilah. Rather, by His wisdom He placed between creation and acquisition a barrier, which is the system of human constitution with what it contains of will, perception and power. This is what His saying ﴿and Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ indicates, meaning: He is Seeing of it before you do it, and after you have done it.

So al-Basir (the Seeing) is intended to mean the Knowing with a knowledge of unveiling that admits no concealment; it is like the knowledge of direct witnessing. This is a common usage in the Qur'an, especially when the attribute al-Basir is mentioned alone without being accompanied by al-Sami' (the Hearing).

Some theologians have established that the attribute of basirah (perception) is: knowing visible things. Others said: it is the connection of divine knowledge to matters at the time they occur. The truth is that these are different usages. By this, the way of reconciling what appears as contradiction between Qur'anic verses and reports from the Sunnah becomes clear. So take this as an exemplar to be followed, and say likewise. Likewise.

This is a precautionary qualification against the supposition that their division into two groups means approval of both conditions, as was related of the polytheists: ﴿And they said: If the All-Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:20).

It is a digression by way of kinaya, through which it alludes to the promise and the threat.

His saying ﴿what you do﴾ includes the deeds of the hearts, such as faith, and these are the primary object intended here.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 64, verse 3:

﴿He created the heavens and the earth﴾.

This is a explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) arising from His saying ﴿Among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ [al-Taghabun: 2]. It explains that their division into the two categories of disbelievers and believers arose from a group of people deviating from the truth upon which the creation of the heavens and the earth was established. This is because the truth is that people should believe in the existence of their Creator and that He is One, and that they should single Him out for worship. That is what God intended from their creation. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. And He said: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the natural disposition (fitrah) of God upon which He created people. There is no alteration in the creation of God﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. Whoever deviates from faith and inclines toward disbelief has deviated from the truth and the natural disposition.

﴿with truth﴾.

His saying ﴿with truth﴾ is a parenthetical phrase (i'tiraD) between the clause ﴿He created the heavens and the earth﴾ and the clause ﴿and He shaped you﴾.

In His saying ﴿with truth﴾ there is an allusion to the affirmation of resurrection and recompense, because His saying "with truth" is connected to the verb "created" by the connection of accompaniment (ta'alluq al-mulabasah), expressed by the preposition bi-, meaning: a creation accompanied by truth. Truth is the opposite of falsehood. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190], up to His saying ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191]. The falsehood that is its counterpart there is futility (al-'abath), by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38] ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39]. So it is established that the referent of truth in His saying ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ is that it is the opposite of futility and purposelessness.

What is meant by ﴿He created the heavens and the earth﴾ is that He created their essences and created what is in them of created things, as indicated by His saying ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38] ﴿We did not create them except with truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 39], meaning: We did not create them and what is between them except with truth. Likewise the estimation (taqdir) in the verse of this surah is to be understood.

The accompaniment of truth to the creation of the heavens and the earth necessarily must be a general and constant accompaniment, because if the accompaniment of truth were broken in any state of the states of the created things of the heavens, it would contradict the meaning of the accompaniment of their creation with truth. So the denial of resurrection for recompense for the deeds of created beings would necessitate

the breakdown of that accompaniment in some states. The non-occurrence of recompense for deeds in this world is observed, for we often see the righteous in distress and we see the people of corruption in comfort. So if this worldly life were the final life of the responsible beings, many people of righteousness would not receive a reward for their righteousness, and most people of corruption would end up enjoying the satisfaction of their wicked souls and the attainment of their desires. Thus the creation of both of these groups would not be accompanied by truth in the intended sense.

To intensify the awakening to this allusion, His saying ﴿and to Him is the final return﴾ is conjoined to it. All of this is a preparation for what preceded it, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those who disbelieve claim that they will never be resurrected﴾ [al-Taghabun: 7].

In His saying ﴿with truth﴾ there is a symbol of recompense, which is both threat and promise.

Also, in His saying ﴿He created the heavens﴾ to the end of the verse there is a manifestation of the greatness of God in His dominion.

﴿And He shaped you and perfected your shapes﴾. This is an incidental insertion (idmaj) of a favour upon people: that together with what they were created upon of the accompaniment of truth in general terms, they have perfection, which is what divine wisdom required. They were created in the best of forms, since the form of the human being is complete in beauty and uniform in it, not afflicted by the monstrosity of some of its parts or the lack of benefit from them, which would spoil the beauties of the rest. This is unlike the finest beauties of animals, such as quadrupeds, birds, and fish, which walk on four limbs with the head generally inverted, or crawl, or hop in their walking in some cases.

Defects do not afflict the human form except from accidents that occur during the period of its formation, such as blows to the wombs of mothers, or diseases that befall them or the foetuses, or from accidents that occur to it during its lifetime, which disfigure some of the beauties of forms. Such things are not counted as part of the original shaping of the human being. Moreover, although such cases are rare, they are not considered monstrosity, but a relative deficiency in beauty. Thus the verse combines an allusion to what wisdom required with a reminder of what bounty required. It also contains an indication of the proof of the possibility of resurrection, as He said: ﴿Were We then wearied by the first creation?﴾ [Qaf: 15], and He said: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ [Ya Sin: 81].

﴿And to Him is the final return﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿and He shaped you﴾, because shaping entails bringing into being, so it is followed by a reminder that after this bringing into being there is annihilation, then resurrection for recompense.

Al-masir is a mimi noun (noun of place/time/event formed with mim) from the verb sara, meaning returned and ended, and for this reason it is followed by the preposition of termination, meaning: your return is to Him, that is, after death, and this is the destiny of gathering for recompense.

The fronting of ﴿ilayhi﴾ before ﴿al-masir﴾ is for the sake of observing the rhyme (ri'ayah al-fasilah), together with conveying concern with the fact that this destiny is connected to God's pure disposal. It is not intended by the fronting to indicate restriction (qasr), because the polytheists do not believe in this destiny at all, let alone claim that it is a destiny to other than Him so that restriction would be needed in response to them.

This clause is more closely connected to the clause ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ than to the clause ﴿and He shaped you and perfected your shapes﴾, as becomes apparent upon reflection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 64, verse 4:

﴿He knows what is in the heavens and the earth, and He knows what you conceal and what you disclose. And Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾

They used to deny the resurrection on the ground that when the parts of the body are scattered, it is impossible to gather them together or to encompass them. ﴿And they say: "When we have become lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [al-Sajdah: 10]. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He knows what is in the heavens and the earth, and He knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ was a refutation of their doubt, meaning: the One who knows what is in the heavens and the earth is not incapable of gathering the scattered parts of the body when He wills to gather them. And the One who knows the secret within a human being, and a secret is finer and more hidden than the scattered particles of bodies, the locations of those minute parts are not hidden from Him. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3] ﴿Yes, [We are] able to put together even his fingertips﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 4].

The intended meaning is His saying ﴿and He knows what you conceal﴾, as is required by the restriction to it in its concluding phrase, ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾, and He did not mention that He knows the deeds of the limbs. Also, because the address is to the polytheists in Makkah according to the preponderant view, and that was before the hypocrites appeared; so His saying ﴿He knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ was not a threat concerning what people hide of disbelief.

As for the conjunction of (﴿and what you disclose﴾), it completes the reminder of the generality of the scope of His knowledge over deeds.

His saying ﴿He knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ has contained both a warning and a promise, looking back to His saying ﴿Among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ [al-Taghabun: 2]. Therefore this sentence is closely connected to the sentence ﴿He it is who created you; among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ [al-Taghabun: 2].

The repetition of the verb (ya'lamu, "He knows") serves to draw attention to this specific scope of divine knowledge after mention of its general scope in His saying ﴿He knows what is in the heavens and the earth﴾, as an alert to the warning and the promise in a particular aspect.

The sentence ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) for the sentence ﴿He knows what you conceal﴾, because He knows what all people among the addressees and others have concealed.

And (dhat al-sudur, "that which is within the breasts") is an adjective of an elided noun which has taken the place of the noun it qualifies, meaning: the companions of the breasts, i.e., the things concealed within them.

The estimated meaning: by the intentions and thoughts "that which is within the breasts," like His saying ﴿and We carried him upon one of planks and nails﴾ [al-Qamar: 13]. Its explanation has already preceded at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [al-Anfal: 43] in Surat al-Anfal.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 64, verse 5:

﴿Has there not come to you the news of those who disbelieved before? So they tasted the bad consequence of their affair, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ This is a transition from the symbolic allusion to the otherworldly threat in His saying (﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ [At-Taghabun: 2]), to His saying (﴿And to Him is the return﴾ [At-Taghabun: 3]), and His saying (﴿He knows what you conceal and what you declare﴾ [At-Taghabun: 4]), to a more explicit allusion than that, by way of hinting at a threat of punishment both worldly and otherworldly together. For what is called in the science of kinayah (metonymy) "allusion by implication" (iyma') has fewer intermediary meanings than "indirect allusion" (ta'rid) and "symbolic allusion" (ramz), so it is closer to explicit statement (tasrih). This hinting through the presentation of an example, by the condition of peoples who received their messengers in the same manner in which the polytheists received Muhammad (ﷺ), is a warning to them lest there befall them the like of what befell those, so the sentence is independent (ibtida'iyyah), because it is an enumeration of a second category of their disbelief, which is the denial of the messengership.

The address is therefore to the specific disbelieving group, by the indication of His saying ﴿those who disbelieved before﴾. This address is directed to the polytheists whose condition is like the condition of those who were not reached by the news of those who disbelieved with the same disbelief as theirs, such as 'Ad, Thamud, Madyan and the people of Ibrahim.

The interrogation is confirmatory (taqriri), and with the confirmatory interrogation the sentence is given in negative form, as a widening of latitude for the one being confronted: if he intends denial, then once he acknowledges, he cannot after his acknowledgment deny, because he has already been excused beforehand by being prompted with the negation; this has been mentioned more than once before.

The noun that "qabl" is attached to has been omitted while its meaning is intended, and the estimate is: (from before you), i.e., in disbelief, by the indication of His saying ﴿So among you is a disbeliever﴾ [At-Taghabun: 2]. The disbelievers know that they are the intended ones, because they are the ones who advance into disbelief and persist in it.

Al-wabal: the evil and what is disliked.

Al-amr: the matter and the state of affairs.

Al-dhawq (tasting) is a metaphor for general perception and feeling; it likens what befell them of punishment to a thing of disagreeable taste that the one it befalls tastes and swallows, because tasting with the tongue is more intense than touching with the hand or the skin. The meaning: they perceived the punishment in this world with a firm perception.

His saying (﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾) is intended to refer to the punishment of the Hereafter, because the conjunction ('atf) requires difference.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 64, verse 6:

﴿That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, but they said, "Shall mere humans guide us?" So they disbelieved and turned away, and Allah was self-sufficient. And Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.﴾

This is an ascent in allusion toward a kind of it that is close to explicit statement, and it is what is called in rhetoric (kinayah) "allusion by indication" (al-ishara). The saying of those before them was similar to the saying of the addressees, so if it was the cause of what they tasted of the calamity, it is likely that those who are similar to them in saying will taste the like of that calamity.

The demonstrative (ism al-ishara) refers to what was mentioned of the calamity and the painful punishment.

This is a counting of another disbelief among the aspects of their disbelief, namely their denial of the Messenger ﷺ and their denial of the Qur'an, for the Qur'an is one of the clear proofs (bayyinat), since it is a miracle (mu'jizah).

The ba' (ba') is causal, in the position of the cause ('illah). The pronoun is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), for the purpose of magnifying what the pronoun explains, which is the clause ﴿their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾ to its end.

The interrogation in (﴿Shall mere humans...?﴾) is an interrogation of denial and nullification. They deemed it impossible that a human like themselves should guide humans like them. This is from their ignorance of the ranks of human souls and of whom Allah chooses from among them and creates qualified to bear the conveyance of His message to His servants, as He said: ﴿And they said, "What is this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7], and they were ignorant that only one of their own kind is fit to guide people. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say, "Had there been in the earth angels walking securely, We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger."﴾ [al-Isra': 95]. When they deemed it impossible that a human could be fit to guide another human like himself, they made that sufficient for their turning away from accepting the Qur'an and reflecting upon it.

Al-Bashar (basha­r): a collective noun for the human being, applying to the singular as in His saying: ﴿Say, "I am only a human like you"﴾ [al-Kahf: 110], and applied to the plural as here. It was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿and they said, "Allah forbid! This is not a human"﴾ [Yusuf: 31] in Surat Yusuf, and in Surat Maryam at His saying ﴿so she presented herself to her a man in form perfect﴾ [Maryam: 17].

The indefiniteness of (﴿basharun﴾ [Al 'Imran: 47]) is for specifying the kind, because the focus of the denial is on their guiding them, and that is the kind of humanity.

The fronting of the predicated subject (al-musnad ilayh) before the verbal predicate is for the purpose of strengthening the judgment of denial. They did not say this until they believed it, and therefore they proceeded to disbelieve in their messengers, since they believed the impossibility of Allah sending them, so they were certain of their lying in the claim of messengerhood. Therefore, the consequence was made upon it (﴿so they disbelieved and turned away﴾).

Al-tawalli (turning away) originally means departing from the place in which you are, and here it is used figuratively for turning away from accepting the call of their messengers. It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 64] in Surat al-Baqarah.

(﴿Wastaghna﴾) means "was free of need." The sin and the ta' are for emphasis (al-mubalaghah), as in His saying (﴿As for he who considers himself self-sufficient﴾ [‘Abasa: 5]). The meaning: Allah was free of need of their faith. He said: ﴿If you disbelieve, indeed Allah is free of need of you﴾ [al-Zumar: 7].

The waw is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), meaning: and the circumstance is that Allah has been free of need of them from a time past, for the freedom of Allah from their faith is established in eternity.

Page 270

It is permissible that what is meant is: "and Allah was free of need" of repeating His call to them, because in what He showed them of clear proofs at the hands of their messengers there was what is sufficient for attaining assent to the call of their messengers were it not for obstinacy; therefore the punishment was hastened upon them.

On both views, the object of (istaghna) is omitted, indicated by His saying (fakafaru, "they disbelieved"), and His saying (bil-bayyinat, "with the clear proofs"). The estimate is: "and Allah was free of need of their faith."

The clause (﴿And Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy﴾) is a concluding appendage (tadhyil): He is free of need of everything in what He demanded of them, and Praiseworthy to whoever complies and gives thanks.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 64, verse 7:

﴿The disbelievers claim that they will never be resurrected. Say: "Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected, then you will surely be informed of what you did. That is easy for God."﴾ This is a third category of the disbelief of the polytheists addressed by His words ﴿Has there not come to you…﴾ [al-Taghabun: 5], etc., namely their disbelief through their denial of resurrection (al-ba'th) and recompense (al-jaza').

The sentence is independent (ibtida'iyyah, a sentence that begins a new statement and is not grammatically attached to what precedes). This speech is directed at the Prophet ﷺ, as indicated by His words ﴿Say, "Yes"﴾. This is neither an instance of using an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (al-izhar fi maqam al-idmar) nor of iltifat (shift of address); rather, it is the beginning of a new purpose, addressed to someone other than those with whom the address had been ongoing.

The sentence contains an explicit affirmation of resurrection. What was previously conveyed concerning it, through His words ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ [al-Taghabun: 3] and His words ﴿He knows what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Taghabun: 4], is as you have just learned.

Al-za'm (claim): a statement marked by its contradiction of reality, an error. Among it is a lie whose speaker did not intend to contradict reality in the estimation of the hearer. It is also applied to a report that is strange and doubtful as to whether what it reports occurred. Shurayh said: "For everything there is a kunya (euphemism), and the kunya of lying is 'they claim'." He meant by kunya the kinayah (indirect expression). Thus between zan and lying there is a partial overlap of general and specific (umum wa khusus wajhi).

In the hadith: "How evil is the mount of a man toward lying: 'they claim'," meaning the saying of a man, "they claim such-and-such."

صفحة ٢٧١
The people of literature narrate that when al-A'sha recited to Qays ibn Ma'dikarib al-Kindi his verse in praise of him:

"I was informed of Qays, and I had not tested him, as they claimed, the best of the people of Yemen,"
Qays became angry and said to him: "This is nothing but a claim."

Because of what accompanies the claim of the speaker's illusion of the truth of what he said, the verb zaʿama is attached to the verbs of opinion (af'al al-zann), so it governs two objects. This is not common in their speech. Among examples is the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"If you claim that I was ignorant among you, then I have exchanged forbearance for ignorance after you."

Among the grammatical evidences is the verse of Abu Umayya Aws al-Hanafi:

"She claimed me an old man, and I am not an old man; the old man is only one who creeps along crawling."

Most commonly, after the verb zaʿama comes an (that), either the open, emphatic form or the light form, as in this verse, so that the verbal noun formed with it takes the place of the two objects. The estimate is: "The disbelievers claimed the negation of their resurrection."

The discussion of the verb zaʿama was preceded in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Have you not seen those who claim that they have believed in what was revealed to you?﴾ [al-Nisa': 60], the verse in surah al-Nisa', and in His words ﴿Then We will say to those who associated partners: Where are your partners whom you used to claim?﴾ [al-An'am: 22], in surah al-An'am. What I have mentioned here is more complete.

By ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ here is meant the polytheists of Makkah and those who follow their religion.

The bringing of the particle (lan) is to emphasize the negation, so they were certain of the negation of resurrection.

For this reason the refutation of their claim was made emphatic by an oath, so that it would overturn their negation with something stronger than it. The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to convey to them from God that resurrection is certain, and He addressed them with this as a record against them, so that they could not say that this had not been conveyed to them.

The clause (﴿Say, "Yes"﴾) is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between the clause (﴿The disbelievers claimed﴾) and the clause (﴿So believe in God and His Messenger﴾) [al-Taghabun: 8].

The particle (bala) is a particle of response used to refute, specific to answering a negative statement in order to refute it.

The clause (﴿then you will surely be informed of what you did﴾) is an escalation in the refutation. The particle (thumma) indicates a rank-based delay (li al-taraakhi al-rutbi), for informing them of what they did is more important than affirming resurrection, since it is the cause of the resurrection.

Al-inba' means informing. Their being informed of what they did is a kinayah for their being called to account for it and recompensed for what they did, for recompense entails that the one recompensed knows the deed for which he is recompensed. Thus the occurrence of recompense is like informing him of what he did, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿To Us is their return, then We will inform them of what they did﴾ [Luqman: 23].

This is a warning and threat of evil recompense, because the context indicates that their deed is evil, namely their denial of the Messenger ﷺ and their rejection of what he called them to.

The clause (﴿and that is easy for God﴾) is a concluding statement (tadhyil), and the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah).

The demonstrative (dhalika) either refers back to the resurrection understood from (﴿you will surely be resurrected﴾), like His words ﴿Be just, that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8], meaning justice is nearer to piety, or it refers to the meaning of the whole that was mentioned: (﴿you will surely be resurrected, then you will surely be informed of what you did﴾).

He described it with (yasir, easy) rather than saying (waqi', certain), as in His words ﴿Indeed, the recompense is certainly to occur﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 6], because the discourse aims to refute their claim that resurrection is impossible on the grounds that the parts of the body have scattered, so that gathering them is impossible. So they were told that what is difficult in the common usage of people is not difficult for God. He has also said in another verse, ﴿And He it is who begins creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27].

﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger and the light that We have sent down. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ This is part of the statement that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to say.

The *fa'* here is *fasihah* (an "eloquent" fa', which makes explicit a condition that is implied), and the implied sense is: "When you have understood these proofs and remembered the punishment that befell your likes, and what you will be informed of regarding your deeds, then believe in Allah, His Messenger, and the Qur'an, meaning its text."

[p. 273]

By "the light that We have sent down" is meant the Qur'an. It is described as "light" by way of metaphor (*istiarah*, a figure in which one thing is named by the name of another on the basis of resemblance), because it resembles light in clarifying what is sought, through the soundness of its argument and the eloquence of its speech. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ [an-Nisa': 174]. It also resembles light in guiding to the upright way, and the divine books share this second resemblance. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]. The indicator (*qarinah*) of the metaphor is His words ﴿that We have sent down﴾, because this is among the features that suit the comparison, since the Qur'an is widely known among all people by titles derived from "sending down" (*inzal*) and "revelation" (*tanzil"*), and both believers and deniers know this. The sending down here is figurative, meaning the conveying of Allah's intent to the Messenger (ﷺ). This was discussed earlier at His words ﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4] in Surah al-Baqarah, and in many other verses.

The belief in the truth of the Qur'an was placed within the scope of the *fa'* of consequence (*tafri'*) because what precedes the *fa'* implied that they had denied the Qur'an, from His words ﴿That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, and they said, "Shall mere humans guide us?"﴾ [at-Taghabun: 6], just as the polytheists of Makkah said. Belief in the Qur'an includes belief in resurrection. Therefore His words ﴿and the light that We have sent down﴾ encompass what preceded the *fa'* in His words ﴿The disbelievers claim that they will never be resurrected﴾ [at-Taghabun: 7], and so on.

In His words ﴿that We have sent down﴾ there is an *iltifat* (a shift from the third person to the first person), to increase the encouragement to believe in the Qur'an by reminding that it was sent down from Allah, because the first-person pronoun indicates its referent more strongly than the third-person pronoun, and to strengthen the call to the one commanded.

The clause ﴿and Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ is a *tadhyil* (a concluding clause that generalizes or reinforces the preceding statement) to the clause ﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. It implies a promise if they believe and a warning if they do not.

Mentioning the name Allah in place of a pronoun is an *izhar fi maqam al-idmar* (the explicit noun used where a pronoun would normally stand), so that the clause stands independently, functioning like a proverb or a comprehensive saying. Also, the explicit noun is stronger in indication than the pronoun, since it does not need to seek a referent. There is in it a cultivation of awe, like the statement of the Caliph, Commander of the Faithful: "He commands you to such-and-such."

*Al-Khabir* means "the All-Knowing." Here the attribute *al-Khabir* is used rather than *al-Basir* (the All-Seeing), because what they know of deeds includes perceptible things and imperceptible things such as beliefs, and among these is belief in resurrection. So it is attached to the attribute that indicates the reach of divine knowledge to all existing things, unlike His words mentioned earlier, ﴿It is He who created you, and among you is the disbeliever and among you is the believer, and Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ [at-Taghabun: 2]. For the disbelief of the disbelievers and the belief of the believers have clear, perceptible effects, so it was attached to the attribute that indicates the reach of divine knowledge to perceptible things.

﴿That is the Day of Mutual Loss (yawm al-taghabun)﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraDh) between the clause ﴿then you will surely be informed of what you did﴾ [al-Taghabun: 7] and its complement, and between the clause ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness, He will remove from him his misdeeds﴾, serving to magnify the awe of this Day, as an indirect threat to the polytheists of loss on that Day, that is, of an evil return.

The use of the demonstrative noun in place of a pronoun is intended to give full emphasis to distinguishing it, together with what the demonstrative of the distant conveys of elevation of rank, as previously stated in His words ﴿That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-taghabun is the verbal noun of ghabanahu, from the pattern of mufa'alah, which indicates the occurrence of an action from two or more sides.

The essential meaning of the pattern mufa'alah is to indicate the occurrence of one action from two or more agents in the manner of sharing in that action.

Al-ghabn is that the seller is given a price less than the true value with which he would compensate its equivalent.

So ghabn ultimately results in the seller's loss in his sale; therefore ghabn is applied to absolute loss figuratively by metonymy (majaz mursal), as in the saying of al-A'sha:

He does not accept a bribe in his judgment, nor does he care about the loss (ghabn) of the loser.

Thus the root of al-taghabun in His words ﴿the Day of Mutual Loss﴾ is not used in its literal sense, since there is no exchange in which there could be ghabn; rather it is used in the sense of loss by way of metonymy.

As for the form of tafa'ul, the majority of exegetes took it in its literal sense of an action occurring from two sides, and explained it as: the people of Paradise defrauded the people of the Fire, since the people of Paradise took Paradise and the people of Hell took Hell. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Hasan. Al-Qurtubi and others understood the words of these imams to mean that al-taghabun is an image (tamthil) of the state of the two parties by the state of two traders, one of whom took the full price and the other took the defrauded price. And His words following it, ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness, He will remove from him his misdeeds﴾ up to His words ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾ [al-Tahrim: 9], are an indication of the intended meaning of both sides. On both meanings, His words ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness﴾ up to ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾ are a detailed account of the two parties. Thus there is in the verse metaphor, comparison and imagery: the metaphor is in the root ghabn, and the imagery is in the form taghabun, which is a compound comparison equivalent to an eloquent simile, since the implied sense is: that is a day like a mutual loss.

A few exegetes (and this is what al-Raghib's words in his Mufradat are interpreted as, and Ibn 'Atiyyah stated explicitly) took the form of tafa'ul to mean abundance and intensity of the action, as in our saying "'Afakallah" and "Tabarak Allah," so it is a metaphor (isti'arah), meaning: a great loss for the disbelievers, since they are the focus of warning.

This is similar in meaning to His words ﴿Those are the ones who bought error in exchange for guidance, so their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His words ﴿O you who believe, shall I direct you to a commerce that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ [al-Saff: 10] and what follows in Surat al-Saff.

Thus the form tafa'ul is used figuratively to express the frequency of the occurrence of loss, by the action of many who are involved.

The speech is a threat to the polytheists of their evil condition on the Day of Gathering, for the meaning is: that is a day of your great, severe loss, by the indication of His words before it ﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger and the light which We have sent down﴾ [al-Taghabun: 8]. The one who causes loss to them is Allah, exalted is He.

Had this intention not been meant, He would not have restricted it to saying that it is a day of mutual loss, for there is in it a great gain for the believers in Allah, His Messenger and the Qur'an. So the construction of this restriction is like His words ﴿so their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The bankrupt is only the one who goes bankrupt on the Day of Resurrection."

The definition of both parts of the sentence ﴿That is the Day of Mutual Loss﴾ conveys a restriction of the subject, i.e., restricting the genus of the Day of Mutual Loss to the Day of Gathering indicated by the demonstrative. This is of the type of restricting the attribute to the qualified, a restriction by claim (qasr idda'i): that is the day of loss, not the days of your markets or anything else, for the unimportance of people's loss in this world made the loss of this world as nothing, and made the Day of Resurrection the one in which the genus of loss is confined.

As for the definite article in His words ﴿al-taghabun﴾, it is the lam of the genus, and in this sense is His words ﴿Say: Indeed the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Zumar: 15], and His words about its opposite ﴿They hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾ [Fatir: 29]. This is the determined interpretation of this verse, and most exegetes passed over it briefly and did not extract from it much. And here I have dug my wells, so that it may fall upon the reader as the clear water falls upon the thirsty, and Allah is the Guide.

﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness, He will remove from him his misdeeds and admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great achievement﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs — those are the companions of the Fire, abiding therein; and wretched is the destination﴾.

These are conjoined to the clause ﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Taghabun: 8], and they are a detailed account of what was summarized in His words ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ [al-Taghabun: 8], which is a concluding clause (tadhyil).

"Man" (من) is conditional and the verb after it is in the future: i.e., whoever among the polytheists believes after this admonition, He will remove from him what he has squandered of his misdeeds.

The misdeeds (al-sayyi'at) refer to disbelief and the corrupt actions that preceded it.

Removing misdeeds (takfir al-sayyi'at) is pardoning them from being held to account, and it is the verbal noun of kaffara, an intensive form of kafara.

Its use became predominant for pardoning what has passed of misdeeds, and its origin is the metaphorical use of covering for removal, like forgiveness (ghufran) as well.

"Righteous" (salihan) is in the accusative as an adjective of a verbal object omitted, whose estimate is: a righteous deed.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read nukaffir and (nudkhilhu) with the nun of majesty, by way of iltifat from the third person to the first person, because the context of promise is a context of address, so the first-person pronoun suits it.

The rest read both with the ya' of the third person, according to the apparent requirement, because the pronoun of the Name of Majesty indicates Allah's care for this group.

The clause (﴿That is the great achievement﴾) is a concluding clause.

His words (﴿But those who disbelieved and denied﴾): i.e., they disbelieved and denied previously, and persisted in their disbelief and denial, so they did not respond to this call, and it is established for them that they are the companions of the Fire.
