So the construction of this restriction is like His words ﴿so their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The bankrupt is only the one who goes bankrupt on the Day of Resurrection."

The definition of both parts of the sentence ﴿That is the Day of Mutual Loss﴾ conveys a restriction of the subject, i.e., restricting the genus of the Day of Mutual Loss to the Day of Gathering indicated by the demonstrative. This is of the type of restricting the attribute to the qualified, a restriction by claim (qasr idda'i): that is the day of loss, not the days of your markets or anything else, for the unimportance of people's loss in this world made the loss of this world as nothing, and made the Day of Resurrection the one in which the genus of loss is confined.

As for the definite article in His words ﴿al-taghabun﴾, it is the lam of the genus, and in this sense is His words ﴿Say: Indeed the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Zumar: 15], and His words about its opposite ﴿They hope for a commerce that will never perish﴾ [Fatir: 29]. This is the determined interpretation of this verse, and most exegetes passed over it briefly and did not extract from it much. And here I have dug my wells, so that it may fall upon the reader as the clear water falls upon the thirsty, and Allah is the Guide.

* * *

﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness, He will remove from him his misdeeds and admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great achievement﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieved and denied Our signs — those are the companions of the Fire, abiding therein; and wretched is the destination﴾.

These are conjoined to the clause ﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Taghabun: 8], and they are a detailed account of what was summarized in His words ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ [al-Taghabun: 8], which is a concluding clause (tadhyil).

"Man" (من) is conditional and the verb after it is in the future: i.e., whoever among the polytheists believes after this admonition, He will remove from him what he has squandered of his misdeeds.

The misdeeds (al-sayyi'at) refer to disbelief and the corrupt actions that preceded it.

Removing misdeeds (takfir al-sayyi'at) is pardoning them from being held to account, and it is the verbal noun of kaffara, an intensive form of kafara.

Its use became predominant for pardoning what has passed of misdeeds, and its origin is the metaphorical use of covering for removal, like forgiveness (ghufran) as well.

"Righteous" (salihan) is in the accusative as an adjective of a verbal object omitted, whose estimate is: a righteous deed.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read nukaffir and (nudkhilhu) with the nun of majesty, by way of iltifat from the third person to the first person, because the context of promise is a context of address, so the first-person pronoun suits it.

The rest read both with the ya' of the third person, according to the apparent requirement, because the pronoun of the Name of Majesty indicates Allah's care for this group.

The clause (﴿That is the great achievement﴾) is a concluding clause.

His words (﴿But those who disbelieved and denied﴾): i.e., they disbelieved and denied previously, and persisted in their disbelief and denial, so they did not respond to this call, and it is established for them that they are the companions of the Fire. For this reason, the subject of the predication about them is expressed by a nominal sentence indicating constancy, because of their longstanding disbelief and denial.

The demonstrative is used for them to distinguish them in a manner whereby no others are confused with them, like His words ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], together with what the demonstrative conveys: that their deserving to be perpetually in the Fire arises from disbelief and denial of Allah's signs. This is a threat.

The clause (And wretched is the destination) is a concluding parenthetical clause, to increase the awe of the threat.

﴿No calamity befalls except by the permission of Allah. And whoever believes in Allah – He guides his heart. And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), moved to after the warning to the polytheists about what will befall them through the loss and gain of the Day when Allah gathers the people, the Day of Reckoning. It is likely also a explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because the threat to the polytheists with the Day of Reckoning arouses in the believers the question of retribution against the polytheists in this world for what the Muslims suffer from their harm in Makkah. They did not cease harming the Muslims, striking them in their bodies and their wealth, and subjecting them to trials between them and their spouses and children.

[Page 279]

So what is meant is the calamities that befell the Muslims from the treatment of the polytheists. Allah informed them of what consoles them concerning that: that Allah knows what afflicts them. Al-Qurtubi said: it was said that the occasion of its revelation was that the disbelievers said, "If what the Muslims are upon were true, Allah would have protected them from calamities."

In the usage of the language, the word muṣībah (calamity) is restricted to what befalls a person of evil and harm, although the root of its verb means whatever befalls a person in general. However, the use of the verb aṣāba (to befall) became predominantly applied to the arrival of evil. It has been said regarding His words ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ [An-Nisa: 79] that attributing the befalling (iṣābah) to good is by way of al-mushākalah (matching/parallelism of wording).

The feminine form of muṣībah is because it is interpreted as ḥādithah (an event). It was already discussed at His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Or when a calamity struck you, although you had struck [the enemy] with twice as much﴾ [Al 'Imran: 165], in Surat Al 'Imran.

Al-idhn (permission): its origin is the authorization of an act for one who does it, and it was applied to the permission to enter a house and removing a barrier, because it is derived from adhina lahu (he gave him ear / listened to his speech). Here it is used metaphorically (isti'arah) for the bringing into existence of the causes of events. These are the causes that, in the ordinary course of the system, lead to the occurrence of happenings, and they are among the effects of Allah's creative action in the system of this world, linking effects to their causes, along with His knowledge of what those causes lead to. Since He is the One who brought the causes into existence and the causes of their causes, and since He had made all of that roots and branches by His knowledge and wisdom, the term al-idhn was applied to that decree and bringing into existence. The resemblance is evident. This is similar in meaning to His words ﴿No calamity strikes in the earth or in yourselves except that it is in a Record before We bring it into being﴾ [Al-Hadid: 22].

The requirement of this metaphor is to bring the reality of worldly changes close to the minds of the Muslims, with brevity of expression because the context is too narrow for prolonged explanation of the causes and reasons, and because most of that is not easily reached by the minds of the community. The purpose of this is to teach the Muslims patience with what calamities of events overcome them, so that their resolve does not weaken, they do not become feeble, and grief does not distract them from their important affairs and the management of their concerns, as He said in Surat al-Hadid (﴿So that you will not despair over what has eluded you﴾ [Al-Hadid: 23]).

Therefore He followed it here with His words (﴿and whoever believes in Allah – He guides his heart﴾), i.e., He guides his heart when a calamity befalls him. The complement was omitted because it is evident from the context, as He said (﴿So do not weaken and do not grieve, and you will be superior if you are believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139] ﴿If you have been touched by a wound, the people have certainly been touched by a similar wound. And these days We alternate among the people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140]).

[Page 280]

The meaning: the believer is trained in Islamic morals and follows the injunctions of Allah, Exalted is He. He is averse to corruption of morals, such as impatience and panic. He receives what calamity befalls him with patience and reflection, reminding himself that life is not free of painful or distressing afflictions. Allah, Exalted is He, said ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 155], ﴿who, when disaster strikes them, say, "Indeed, we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 156], ﴿those upon whom are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and those are the guided﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 157], i.e., the people of perfect guidance, because it is guidance received from the true divine teachings, protected from error, like His words here ﴿He guides his heart﴾.

This statement, in His words ﴿and whoever believes in Allah – He guides his heart﴾, is an allusion (iyma') to the command to steadfastness and patience when calamities descend, because it necessarily follows from Allah's guidance of the believer's heart at the time of calamity that the believers are encouraged to be steadfast and to show patience when calamities descend. Therefore it is concluded with the sentence ﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾. It is a tadhyil (concluding sentence) for the preceding sentence, aimed at taking into account everything it contains: that calamities are by the permission of Allah, that Allah guides the hearts of the believers to steadfastness when calamities descend, and the command to steadfastness and patience at the time of calamities. That is, He knows all of that.

In it there is a kinayah (allusion by implication) to the recompense of the patient with reward, because the benefit of Allah's knowledge that concerns people is the cultivation of good character and the hope for reward and the raising of ranks.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 64, verse 12:

﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger. But if you turn away, then upon Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿And whoever believes in Allah – He guides his heart﴾ [al-Taghabun: 11], because that clause implies that the believers are prepared to obey Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) in what they call them to of righteous deeds, as is indicated by the concluding statement of the discourse, ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ [al-Taghabun: 13]. It is also because the demand for obedience is a branch (farʿ) of the realization of faith, as in the hadith of Muʿadh, that when the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him to Yemen he said to him: "You will come to a people who are People of the Book, so the first thing you call them to is that they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. If they obey you in that, then inform them that Allah has enjoined upon them a charity (ṣadaqah)," and the hadith continues.

The branching (tafrīʿ) of ﴿But if you turn away﴾ is a warning against disobedience to Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ).

The word tawallī (turning away) is used metaphorically for disobedience and for not accepting the Messenger's call.

The real meaning of tawallī is departing from the place in which one is settled, and tawallī was borrowed for disobedience in order to denounce it, as an intensification in warning against it. Similar to this is the Exalted's saying in addressing the believers: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people other than you﴾ [Muhammad: 38], and He said: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you are hearing﴾ [al-Anfal: 20].

The definiteness in His saying ﴿Our Messenger﴾ by the construct (iḍāfa) is for the purpose of magnifying his status, that he (ﷺ) is the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds. And this pronoun is an iltifāt (shift) from the third person to the first person, which conveys the honouring of the Messenger through the dignity of being attributed to the speaker.

The meaning of restriction (ḥaṣr) in His saying (﴿So upon Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾) is the restriction of the Messenger (ﷺ) to the state of his obligation being conveyance; it is the restriction of a described entity to an attribute: the Messenger (ﷺ) is restricted to the necessity of conveyance for him, not exceeding that to the necessity of anything else. This is a restriction of correction (qaṣr qalb), treating them, in the state of disobedience that is supposed, as those who believe that Allah, if He willed, would have compelled them to act upon what He commanded them, spurring their souls to obedience through urging.

The description of ﴿conveyance﴾ as ﴿clear﴾ means evident, a proof of excuse for the Messenger (ﷺ), in that he claimed what he was commanded in the most complete manner, cutting off the excuse of those who fail to comply with what they were commanded.

And in terms of the concept of restriction, the clause ﴿So upon Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾ serves as the answer to the condition without need of postulating an answer for which this clause would be evidence or cause.

Allah — there is no god but Him.

This is a parenthetical sentence (jumla mu'taridha) placed between the clause "And obey Allah and obey the Messenger" (al-Taghabun 64:12) and the clause "And upon Allah let the believers put their trust."

The name Allah (ism al-jalala) is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause "there is no god but Him" (la ilaha illa huwa) is the predicate (khabar). This is a reminder to the believers of what they already know: that whoever believes that Allah — there is no god but Him — it is incumbent upon him to obey Him and not to heed what afflicts him, in the way of obeying Allah, of calamities and harm, as Khubayb ibn 'Adi said:

"I care not, when I am slain as a Muslim, on which side I fall for the sake of God."

It is also permissible that the clause "Allah — there is no god but Him" occupies the position of a cause (ta'lil) for the clause "And obey Allah" (al-Taghabun 64:12), and it also gives the reason for the clause "And obey the Messenger" (al-Taghabun 64:12), because obedience to the Messenger returns to obedience to Allah, as He, the Exalted, said: "Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah" (al-Nisa' 4:80).

The opening of the clause with the name Allah is a noun in the place of a pronoun (izhar fi maqam al-idmar), since he did not say "He, there is no god but He," in order to evoke the greatness of Allah, the Exalted, through the meanings of perfection contained in the name Allah, and so that the clause stands independently by itself, thereby functioning like proverbs and comprehensive sayings (al-kalim al-jawami').

* * *

"And upon Allah let the believers put their trust" is coordinated (ma'tuf) on "And obey Allah" (al-Taghabun 64:12). Its meaning is: "And put your trust in Allah," for the believers put their trust in Allah and not in other than Him; and since you are believers, put your trust in Him.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase (taqdim al-majrur) serves to convey exclusivity (ikhtisas), meaning: the believers do not put their trust except in Allah.

In this, the form of a command to the believers to trust in Allah alone, rather than others, is used, to strengthen their hearts (rabt 'ala qulubihim) and to steady their souls, so that they do not grieve over the turning away of the polytheists and what they suffer from them, and that this will not harm them.

For the believers do not take pride in them nor seek strength through their likes, because Allah has commanded them not to trust except in Him. This also indicates that they do not oppose the command of Allah, and that enrages the disbelievers.

The use of the name Allah in His saying "And upon Allah let the believers put their trust" is a noun in the place of a pronoun, so that the clause stands independently and runs like a proverb. For this reason the word "the believers" (al-mu'minun) was stated explicitly, and he did not say "And upon Allah let them put their trust," and because the word "the believers" carries the comprehensive generality that includes both the addressees and others, so that the sense of exemplification (al-tamthil) is achieved.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 64, verse 14:

﴿O you who have believed, indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon and overlook and forgive, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Page 283

An turning toward the address to the believers with that which benefits them in perfection and keeps them away from that which would tempt them.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that a man asked him about this verse, and he said: "These were men from the people of Makkah who embraced Islam and wanted to come to the Prophet ﷺ, but their spouses and children refused to let them go. When they came to the Prophet ﷺ after a period, their spouses and children came with them. They saw that the people had become learned in the religion, meaning they had preceded them in understanding of the religion because these had delayed in migrating. So they intended to punish them for what they had caused them, until the people outstripped them in understanding of the religion. Then Allah revealed this verse, up to His saying ﴿But if you pardon and overlook and forgive, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾." This is what al-Wahidi relied upon in (his book) Asbab al-Nuzul, and its implication is that the verse is Medinan.

And from 'Ata' ibn Yasar and Ibn 'Abbas also: that this verse was revealed in Medina concerning 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, who had a family and children. Whenever he wanted to go on a raid, they wept before him and softened him, saying: "To whom will you leave us?" So he would feel pity for them and stay back from the raid. He complained of that to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse was revealed concerning them. So this verse is a fresh, initiatory resumption, and its placement here is that its revelation as a cause coincided with its occurrence right after what preceded it from this surah.

Its connection with the verse before it is that both are a consolation for what afflicted the believers of grief from the treatment of their enemies toward them, and from the deviation of some of their spouses and children against them.

If the whole surah is Meccan, as is the view of al-Dahhak, then the verse is the beginning of a turning toward addressing the believers specifically after fulfilling the purpose with which the surah began, according to the Qur'an's custom of following topics with their opposites, of encouragement or warning, praise or blame, or the like, so that both sides receive their due. It was also an alert to the Muslims regarding circumstances within their families that might be hidden from them, so that they would take their precaution. This is the fitting context for the period before the Hijrah, when the Muslims in Makkah were intermingled with the polytheists through ties of lineage, marriage and alliance. When the polytheists took hostility toward them for leaving their religion and harbored resentment against them, and they became two factions, each faction was not free of individuals varying in hostility according to the variation in firmness of religion and in the bonds of kinship and marriage. Hostility may reach its extreme, so that all bonds are dissolved before it, and the closest relative becomes the most harmful to his kin more than a distant one would be.

This verse awakened the believers lest their relatives deceive them in what was assumed to be a source of deception, so that their harm would be more severe upon them. In this awakening there is a benefit for the religion and for the Muslims. For this reason Allah the Exalted said ﴿so beware of them﴾ and did not command that they harm them, and He followed it with His saying ﴿But if you pardon and overlook and forgive, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, combining caution with peaceful dealing, and that is from prudence.

And (min) is partitive. The fronting of the predicate of (inna) before its subject is for emphasis on this predicate, and for the suspense it creates toward the subject, so that the content of this predicate settles in the mind most completely, because of its strangeness and importance. A similar construction occurred earlier at His saying ﴿And among the people is one who says: We believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8] in Surat al-Baqarah.

(ʿaduww) is a descriptive noun from enmity (al-ʿadawah) on the pattern faʿul in the sense of fa'il, and therefore it remains in the singular and masculine form when used as an adjective. This was discussed at His saying ﴿If he was from a people hostile to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 92] in Surat al-Nisa'. But when it is intended in the sense of a noun, it agrees with what it describes, as He the Exalted said ﴿They will be enemies to you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 2].

Describing some spouses and children as enemies may be taken literally, for some of them may harbor enmity toward their spouse, and some toward their parents, because of treatment that does not please them, together with corruption of the soul and poor thinking, so that he becomes an enemy to one who should be a friend to him. Such enmity often comes from difference of religion and from alignment with the enemies.

It may also be understood as an eloquent simile, meaning: like an enemy in conduct, by doing what is the manner of enemies' treatment, as it is said in the proverb: "The ignorant person does to himself what the enemy does to his enemy." This is the use of a word in both its literal and figurative senses.

Joined to His saying (﴿so beware of them﴾) is the clause (﴿But if you pardon and overlook﴾) to its end, by way of a precautionary conjunction (ʿatf al-ihtiras), because if pardon is desired and beloved to Allah the Exalted, and it occurs only after the sin has taken place, then the absence of accountability for a mere suspicion of enmity is more deserving of seeking. Thus what is understood is a prohibition against treating spouses and children as enemies because of the suspicion of enmity. Rather, the purpose of the warning is precaution and taking care to prevent the beginning of accountability. For this reason it was said: "Prudence is harboring bad thoughts about people," meaning: but without building upon that suspicion the treatment of one from whom what you suspected has come. Allah the Exalted said (﴿Indeed, some suspicion is sin﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12]) and said (﴿lest you harm a people in ignorance and then become regretful for what you have done﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6]).

Pardon (al-'afw) is abandoning punishment for a sin after being prepared for it, even with reproach.

Overlooking (al-safh) is turning away from the wrongdoer, that is, abandoning his punishment for his sin without reproach.

Forgiving (al-ghafr) is concealing the sin and not spreading it.

Their being combined here is an indication of the gradation of the effects of this enmity and of what its effects require of these three kinds of treatment. The object of the three verbs is omitted, because it is evident that what is meant is your children and spouses in what proceeds from them that harms you. It is also possible that the omission of the object is to intend the generality of encouragement toward pardon.

A person pardons, overlooks, and forgives the wrongdoer only when his wrong relates to that person's right. The actions mentioned here are stated absolutely, while the texts of the Shari'ah contain restrictions upon them.

The clause (﴿Then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾) is the evidence for an omitted conditional answer that conveys encouragement toward pardon, overlooking and forgiveness. The sense is: "And if you pardon, overlook and forgive, Allah loves that from you, because Allah is Forgiving and Merciful," meaning toward those who forgive and show mercy. The attribute (Merciful) comprises the three qualities.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 64, verse 15:

﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial, and Allah has with Him a great reward.﴾

This is a concluding generalization (tadhyil), because it generalizes the condition of children after a particular condition of some of them was mentioned.

Wealth is incorporated (idmaj) into it, because it is not covered by the command to beware nor by the description of enmity. The mention of wealth is placed before children because wealth had not been mentioned earlier, unlike children.

The reason for incorporating wealth here is that the Muslims had been struck in their wealth by the polytheists, who overcame them in their possessions, and wealth was not mentioned in the previous verse because the aim there is warning against the things most closely attached to them, namely their spouses and their children. Moreover, the trial of these is doubled, because the one who calls to it comes from themselves and from the efforts and embellishments of others. The mention of spouses is omitted here, being sufficed by the indication of the trial of children upon them through the implication of the discourse (dalalat fahwa al-khitab), for their trial is more severe than the trial of children, because their boldness in embellishing things to their husbands and what they attempt with them is greater than the boldness of children.

The restriction (qasr) conveyed by (inna) is the restriction of the described upon a description, i.e., your wealth and your children are nothing but a trial. It is an restriction by claim (qasr idda'i) for the sake of exaggeration in the frequency of this attribute's accompanying the described, since it is rare for individuals of these two kinds, namely the wealth and children of Muslims, to be free of the attribute of trial for whoever is afflicted by them.

The predication with "﴿fitnatun﴾ (a trial)" is for exaggeration. What is meant is that they are a cause of trial, whether or not they strive in the commission of trials, for preoccupation with wealth and care for children contain trial.

In this verse, then, among the special features of the science of meanings (ilm al-ma'ani) are tadhyil and idmaj, both of which belong to elaboration (itnab), and sufficiency (iktifa'), which belongs to brevity (ijaz). It also contains the predication with the verbal noun, which is "﴿fitnatun﴾", and predication with it is a form of exaggeration. These are four of the embellishments of rhetoric (muhassinat badi'iyya). It also contains restriction (qasr) and causal explanation (ta'lil), which is among the special features of disjunction (fasl), and which may also be counted among the embellishments of rhetoric. These are six special features.

This sentence is disjoined (fusilat) from the one before it, because it includes tadhyil and ta'lil, and both of these are requirements of disjunction.

Fitna (trial): the agitation and bewilderment of the soul due to circumstances that do not suit the one they befall. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And trial is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqara: 191] in Surat al-Baqara.

Abu Dawud related from Buraydah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was delivering a sermon on Friday when al-Hasan and al-Husayn came stumbling and getting up. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ descended from the pulpit, took them, pulled them to him, then recited ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾. And he said: 'I saw these two and could not be patient,' then he resumed his sermon."

Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned that 'Umar said to Hudhayfa: "How did you wake up?" He said: "I woke up loving trial and hating the truth." 'Umar said: "What is this?" He said: "I love my child and I hate death."

His saying ﴿and Allah has with Him a great reward﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon the clause ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾, because His saying ﴿with Him is a great reward﴾ is a metonymy (kinaya) for the recompense for that trial for whoever restrains himself from complying with what it embellishes for him of deviation from the pleasure of Allah, if there is embellishment in that. The great reward is for giving the right of wealth and for compassion toward children, i.e., Allah will reward you for them. This is in accordance with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever is tested with these daughters with something, they will be a screen for him from the Fire." And in another hadith: "Patience upon the bad character of a wife is an act of worship."

The hadiths on this meaning are numerous, among them what Hudhayfa related: "The trial of a man regarding his family and his wealth is expiated by prayer and charity."

﴿So fear God as much as you are able, and listen and obey, and spend for your own good. Whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful.﴾

The fa' here is *fa' fasihah* (the fa' that introduces a clause implied by what precedes it), and it marks a consequence of what came before. The meaning is: since you know this, fear God in what is required of taqwa (God-consciousness and piety) in dealing with children and spouses, and in the disposal of wealth. Do not let love for these things, and preoccupation with them, prevent you from your obligations. Do not let anger or the like take you beyond the bounds of the justice commanded. Nor should love of wealth prevent you from paying the rights attached to wealth or from seeking it by lawful means. The command to taqwa therefore includes the warning mentioned earlier, the encouragement to forgiveness as mentioned before, and everything beyond that.

The address is to the believers.

The omission of the object of (ittaqu, "fear") is intended to generalise what relates to taqwa across all the states mentioned and others. For this reason, this statement serves as a *tadhyil* (a concluding summary), because its meaning is more general than what precedes it.

Since taqwa concerning the matters mentioned and others may be neglected by its bearer, through eagerness to satisfy the desires of the soul in many of these matters, the command to taqwa is reinforced by the words (﴿as much as you are able﴾).

Here *ma* is a verbal-masdar (*masdariyyah zarfiyyah*), meaning "for the duration of your ability," so that it covers all times and all states, and covers all abilities. Thus they should not abandon taqwa at any time. The times were made the time-frame (*zarf*) of ability so that they do not fall short through neglect in anything they are able to do, in matters they have been commanded to be mindful of, so long as it does not go beyond the limit of ability into hardship. God says: ﴿God desires ease for you and does not desire hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

So there is in His words ﴿as much as you are able﴾ no lightening and no tightening, but it is justice and fairness. It contains what is incumbent upon them and what is for their benefit.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "I pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to hear and obey, and he taught me: 'as much as you are able.'" And from Ibn 'Umar: "When we pledged allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ) to hear and obey, he would say to us: 'as much as you are able.'"

The conjunction of (﴿and listen and obey﴾) to (ittaqu Allah, "fear God") is *'atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm* (the specific joined to the general), for the sake of giving it importance. Also, taqwa is understood primarily as abstaining from what is forbidden, since it is derived from *waqa* (to protect). Thus the taqwa of God means that a person protects himself from what God has forbidden him. But since abandoning the commanded acts leads to committing forbidden acts, because abandoning a command is itself forbidden (for commanding something is a prohibition of its opposite), mentioning it explicitly was a matter of importance for both matters, so that the true legal taqwa is realised, which is avoiding what is forbidden and carrying out what is commanded.

The meaning is: listen to God, that is, obey by listening to the Messenger (ﷺ) and obeying him.

The command to listen is a command to receive the Sharia and to attentively hear the admonitions of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that is a means to taqwa. God says: ﴿So give good news to My servants﴾ [al-Zumar: 17] ﴿who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾ [al-Zumar: 18].

Joined to it is (﴿and obey﴾) [al-Taghabun: 12]: that is, obey what you have heard of command and prohibition.

The conjunction of (﴿and spend﴾) is a specification after a specification, for spending is among what God has commanded, and so it is among the commanded acts.

The form of the imperative includes obligatory spending and recommended spending, so there is in it encouragement to spend in both its degrees. This is part of the concern for purity from the temptation of wealth mentioned in His words: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Taghabun: 15].

(﴿Khayran﴾, "good") is in the accusative as a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun indicated by (anfiqu, "spend"). The estimate is: spend good spending for your own benefit. This is the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', in which case *khayr* is an elative noun (*ism tafdil*). Its original form is *akhyar*, with the hamza dropped due to frequent use. The meaning is: spending is better for you than withholding. From Sibawayh, however, it is accusative as an object of an implied verb indicated by (anfiqu). The estimate is: bring good for your own souls.

The clause (﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾) is a *tadhyil* (concluding summary).

The generality indicates that *man* is intended to refer to a class, not to a specific individual or a particular group. This is a love that is driven by the eagerness of most people to preserve and hoard wealth and to give little of its benefit to others. That eagerness is called *shuhh* (avarice).

The meaning is: spending protects its doer from the forbidden avarice. So when spending in what God has commanded becomes easy for a person, he has been protected from the stinginess of his soul, and that is a form of success.

Since that is a great success, it was expressed with the form of restriction by means of defining the predicate (*qasr* by *ta'rif al-musnad*, i.e., restriction of exclusivity). This restricts the class of the successful to the class of those who were protected from the stinginess of their own souls. It is a *qasr idda'i* (a claimed or rhetorical restriction), for the sake of emphasising the realisation of the description of the successful, namely those protected from the stinginess of their souls. The success of others is thereby made equivalent to non-existence.

The attribution of (*shuhh*, "stinginess") to the soul (*nafs*) points to the fact that stinginess is part of the soul's nature, for souls are stingy with the things they love. God says: ﴿And souls have been made to be prone to stinginess﴾ [al-Nisa': 128].

In a hadith, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about the best charity, he said: "That you give charity while you are healthy and stingy, fearing poverty and hoping for wealth. A parallel of (﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾) [al-Hashr: 9] has already been mentioned in Surah al-Hashr.

This is an explanatory resumptive statement (*istinaf bayani*, a sentence that anticipates a question the hearer may raise), arising from His words: ﴿And spend out of good for yourselves﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]. The multiplying of the reward for spending, together with forgiveness, is a great good. By this placement the listener understands that the word "loan" (*qard*) is applied to the commanded spending by way of metaphor (*isti'ara*). The purpose is to draw attention to the excellence of the commanded spending.

It is emphasized again. After it was made "good," it was made the cause of success, and it was described as a loan from the servant to his Lord. This alone is an encouragement and a gentle way of soliciting, since the one who spends is treated as though he were giving Allah, the Exalted, money. This is part of the meaning of *ihsan* (excellence) in the servant's dealing with his Lord. The Prophet ﷺ explained it in the hadith of Jibril, when "Jibril said to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon them both: 'Tell me about *ihsan*.' The Prophet ﷺ said: '*Ihsan* is that you worship Allah as though you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then He sees you.'" Among what falls under the meaning of worshipping Allah as one who sees Him is that the servant senses that carrying out his Lord's command to spend is, in effect, a transaction between a lender and a borrower.

This was already mentioned at His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a good loan, so He may multiply it for him many times over?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read ﴿yudaa'ifhu﴾ with an *alif* after the *dad*. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read (*yudda'ifahu*), with a shadda on the 'ain, the imperfect of *da''afa*. Both have the same meaning, which is the verbal sense of doubling.

*Al-mudaa'afa* (multiplying) means giving the double (*al-dif*), which is the like of a thing in essence or attribute. It may be satisfied by one like, and after it come more likes, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿many times over﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245].

Spending was made a cause of forgiveness, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Charity extinguishes sins as water extinguishes fire."

*Al-Shakur* is on the pattern *fa'ul* in the sense of *fa'il*, for intensity, meaning one who gives much thanks. The word "thanks" (*shukr*) is applied to it in the sense of recompense with good for doing righteous deeds, by way of likening the action of the one who bestows favour to the recompense of the one who is thanked for a blessing. Yet there is no blessing upon Allah in what His servants do of righteous deeds, for their benefit returns to themselves. But Allah, out of grace, did this to urge them toward their own goodness. So He arranged for them a reward of delight in return for purifying their souls, and He treated them kindly, so that this reward is called "thanks," and He made Himself the One who gives thanks.

[Page 291]

This purpose is indicated by following the attribute *Shakur* with the attribute *Halim* (Forbearing), as an alert that this is part of His forbearance toward His servants, while they have no right over Him, glory be to Him.

As for the description with ﴿knower of the unseen and the seen, the Mighty, the Wise﴾, it completes the reminder of Allah's greatness, and it also suits the encouragement and warning that all the preceding verses contain. This is because the One who knows deeds, both outward and inward, does not let any of the recompense for them escape, which He has arranged for them. And because the Mighty is not overcome by anything.

*Al-Hakim* (the Wise) is the one described with wisdom, who never leaves dealing with people except by what wisdom requires, namely placing things in their proper places and attaching matters to what suits their realities.

*Al-Hakim* is on the pattern *fa'il* in the sense of *al-muhkim*, meaning the one who perfects, in His making and His dealing. Both meanings are among His attributes, may He be exalted, so it is an attribute combining both meanings.

Surat al-Talaq

The surah is widely known in the mushafs, in books of tafsir and in books of Sunnah as "Surat al-Talaq," from His words, "O Prophet, when you divorce women" [al-Talaq: 1], and so on. Its name in this form has not come in any hadith from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that is established as widely accepted.

It is mentioned in *al-Itqan* that Abdullah ibn Mas'ud called it "Surat al-Nisa' al-Qusra" (the shorter Surat al-Nisa'), relying on what al-Bukhari and others narrated from Malik ibn 'Amir, who said: "We were with Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and it was mentioned in his presence that a pregnant woman whose husband has died observes the waiting period of whichever of the two terms is longer: the time of delivery if it is more than four months and ten days, or the four months and ten days. He said: 'Do you impose strictness on her and not grant her the concession? The Surat al-Nisa' al-Qusra was revealed after the Tuwla (the longer one): ﴿and for those with child, their term is until they deliver their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4].'" End of quote. In *al-Itqan*, from al-Dawudi, there is a denial that this surah should be called "al-Qusra," in order to keep the Qur'an free of any description of deficiency. Ibn Hajar refuted this, saying that "shortness" (*qasr*) is a relative matter, that is, it does not imply deficiency in an absolute sense. Ibn Mas'ud described it as "al-Qusra" to distinguish it from the surah known as Surat al-Nisa', which is the fourth surah in the mushaf, beginning with ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul﴾ [al-Nisa': 1]. As for his words "al-Tuwla" (the longer), it is an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning "after the longer surah," that is, Surat al-Baqarah, because it is the longest of the surahs of the Qur'an. It is certain that this is what he meant, because Surat al-Baqarah is the one in which the waiting period of the widow is mentioned. It may be supposed that Surat al-Baqarah is called "the longer Surat al-Nisa'" from its contrast with "the shorter Surat al-Nisa'" in Ibn Mas'ud's speech. But this is not so, as was explained earlier in the commentary on Surat al-Nisa'.

It is Medinan by agreement.

[Page 293]

The number of its verses is twelve according to the majority count. The people of Basra counted it as eleven verses.

It is counted as the ninety-sixth in the order of revelation of the surahs according to Jabir ibn Zayd. It was revealed after Surat al-Insan and before Surat al-Bayyinah.

The occasion of its revelation is what Muslim narrated through the route of Ibn Juraij, from Abu al-Zubayr, that he heard Abd al-Rahman ibn Ayman asking Ibn 'Umar: "How do you view a man who divorced his wife while she was menstruating?" He said: "Ibn 'Umar divorced his wife while she was menstruating in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and 'Umar asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said to him: 'Let him take her back.' So he took her back, and said: 'When she becomes pure, let him divorce her, or let him keep her.'" Ibn 'Umar said: "The Prophet recited: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at their waiting period﴾ [al-Talaq: 1]."

The apparent meaning of his words "The Prophet ﷺ recited, etc." is that the surah was revealed to him at that very time. It is possible that it was revealed before this incident. Al-Wahidi said, on the authority of al-Suddi, that it was revealed concerning the matter of Ibn 'Umar's divorce. And on the authority of Qatada, that it was revealed because the Prophet ﷺ divorced Hafsa, but this is not authentic. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi affirmed that none of that is authentic, and that the most correct view is that the verse was revealed to explain a newly instituted ruling.

The purpose of the verses of this surah is to define the rulings of divorce and what follows from it: the waiting period, nursing, maintenance and housing. It completes the rulings mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

It also contains an indication of the wisdom behind the legislation of the waiting period, and a prohibition against harming divorced women and constricting them.

It contains the call to witness the divorce and the taking back, and the nursing of a divorced woman's son in return for a wage paid by Allah.

It contains the command to consult and to confer between the parents regarding the affairs of their children.

Interspersed with that command to observe these rules is the promise that Allah supports those who fear Allah, follow His limits, make ease in their affairs for them, and remove their misdeeds.

And that Allah has set a ruling for everything, and nothing prevents Him from carrying out His rulings.

This is followed by an admonition through the condition of the nations who rebelled against the command of Allah and His messengers. It is an urging to the Muslims to act upon what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have commanded them, lest the description of rebellion against the command be applied to them.

And it honours the revelation of Allah, may He be exalted, by describing it as sent down from the heavens and issuing from the knowledge and power of Allah, may He be exalted.
